summary: Defines a MIB module for managing the User Datagram Protocol over IPv6, part of a series of IPv6 MIB documents. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 4113 and RFC 8096.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a list of counters that tell a network manager how many UDP messages are going over the new kind of internet addresses.

what is the ipv6 udp mib
how to manage udp over ipv6
subtitle: MIB module for monitoring UDP traffic over IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: Network managers need to monitor UDP on IPv6 networks, but the existing UDP monitoring tools only work with IPv4 addresses.
tldr.mechanism: This MIB defines a new table that represents UDP endpoints using IPv6 addresses, keeping the existing IPv4 tools intact while adding IPv6 support.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is now historic and has been replaced by RFC 4113 and RFC 8096, which provide more comprehensive management approaches.

today: RFC 2454 is Historic and has been replaced by RFC 4113 and RFC 8096. It provides the first standard management approach for UDP endpoints over IPv6, but newer approaches have superseded it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Network management requires the ability to monitor and track protocol activity. A Management Information Base (MIB) is a standard collection of values that management software can read from devices. The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) is used to transmit this information from agents running on managed devices to management stations.

RFC 2454 defines a MIB module specifically for managing UDP (User Datagram Protocol) running over IPv6. This document is part of a series that extends the IPv6 management infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is like a checklist a manager reads to see how a computer is doing. This one is for checking UDP when it runs on new IPv6 addresses.

sections.title: UDP Over IPv6
sections.content:
UDP is a simple datagram protocol that works the same way whether it runs over IPv4 or IPv6. The transport layer, where UDP operates, does not fundamentally change when the underlying IP version changes.

RFC 2454 recommends that most existing UDP MIB objects defined in RFC 2013 are sufficient for both IPv4 and IPv6. For example, the counter for total UDP datagrams delivered to users counts datagrams from both IPv4 and IPv6 without distinguishing between them. This approach minimizes changes to existing IPv4 implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP acts basically the same way whether it carries messages with old or new internet addresses. The counters that measure how much traffic there is work the same for both.

sections.title: Representing IPv6 UDP Endpoints
sections.content:
The one exception is the UDP listener table. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, which cannot be represented using the older IpAddress type used in the original UDP MIB. The standard UDP table, defined in RFC 2013, cannot represent all UDP endpoints that listen on IPv6 addresses.

To solve this problem while leaving IPv4-only implementations untouched, RFC 2454 defines a separate new table called ipv6UdpTable. This table represents only UDP endpoints using IPv6 addresses. UDP endpoints on IPv4 addresses continue to be represented in the existing udpTable.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way of writing down which mailboxes are listening only works for old addresses. So instead of changing the old list, we made a new list just for the new kind of addresses.

sections.title: The IPv6 UDP Table
sections.content:
The ipv6UdpTable contains entries for each UDP endpoint listening on an IPv6 address. Each entry is indexed by three values: the local IPv6 address, the local port number, and an interface index.

The interface index is needed because IPv6 addresses on a managed node are not always globally unique. An address like ::0 (meaning any IPv6 address) may be listening on multiple interfaces, so the table needs the interface identifier to distinguish one endpoint from another.

The table includes one read-only object: ipv6UdpIfIndex, which identifies the local interface associated with the listener. This allows network managers to determine exactly which interface each UDP endpoint is bound to.
sections.plainLanguage: The new table keeps track of which numbered mailboxes are listening on which network ports, so a manager can see where UDP messages are arriving and leaving.

sections.title: Standards and Evolution
sections.content:
RFC 2454 defines conformance statements for MIB implementations. It specifies which objects must be supported by SNMPv2 entities that implement UDP over IPv6.

RFC 2454 is classified as Historic. It has been replaced by RFC 4113 and RFC 8096, which provide updated and more comprehensive approaches to managing UDP and IP traffic over IPv6. The RFC authors anticipated that the objects in RFC 2454 would eventually be incorporated into an updated UDP MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: This document was the first attempt at a checklist for IPv6 UDP management. Later versions improved on it, so this one is no longer used.
